what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: End replies with the thread's state, not quotes
sections.para: Every reply carries the whole thread below it, redundant for a reader who already has it. Instead, a reply should end with a short state of the thread written for this reader: where things are, decisions, open items, next steps, who is on copy, and links. The format is personal, so the article ends with an experiment.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: A sender-written tail beats quoted walls and AI summaries
sections.para: The quoted wall is redundant and clients hide it anyway; the space under a reply should say where we are, what was decided, what is open, what is next and who is on copy. Unlike client AI summaries, the tail is reviewed by the sender and the same for everyone. Agents can draft it, and the format will be tested.

sections.label: The wall, and what it costs
sections.line: Clients send the quoted wall, then hide it
sections.para: Below every reply sit all earlier messages, which the reader already has; Gmail and Apple Mail fold them away. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index found workers receive 117 emails a day, most skimmed in under 60 seconds. The wall holds the raw material for the reader's questions but answers none, especially on a phone.

sections.label: The proposal: end with the state, not the history
sections.line: Six rows give each reader the thread's current state
sections.para: The tail has rows for where we are, decided, open, next, on copy and sources. Sources links back to the condensed messages, making the tail a checkable derived view, not a copy. It is written per reader: the same messages condense differently for the counterparty, a newly added lawyer and a long-standing colleague.

sections.label: What others have done, and where the pieces came from
sections.line: Every piece has precedent, but not the sender-written tail
sections.para: RFC 1855 in 1995 asked for summaries instead of quotes, and AR 25-50, Minto's pyramid and Nygard's decision records share the shape. Superhuman, Shortwave, Copilot, Apple Intelligence and Gmail now summarise threads privately for the reader. A sender-written, recipient-specific tail is accountable and shared; a MailFathom ThreadState issue from August 2026 comes closest.

sections.label: Who writes it
sections.line: The drafts role writes the tail; a person sends
sections.para: The inbox role already captures decisions, questions and statuses as typed blocks, which the drafts role can render into the tail with message ids; a person edits and sends, which no agent does. The tail is correctable, personal via a CRM preference row, and text first. The Cc row exposes who joined and which participants are agents.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.line: A month-long trial tests four tail formats
sections.para: Prose, labelled rows, an ASCII timeline and an HTML card rotate by thread across a month of Dinis's correspondence via the agent@riskmandate.ai team. Measures include whether readers open quotes anyway, follow-up confusion, edits before sending and reply times. Failure signs are stated in advance, and results will be published either way.

sections.label: What exists today, and what does not
sections.line: Inputs exist now; automatic tails and data do not
sections.para: Already running: typed blocks in Email-FS, the drafts role with hashes and Sent-folder records, per-contact CRM folders, reader-side summaries in major clients, and hand-written tails. Missing: automatic tails with Cc changes, the preference row, variant templates, the measurement report, the month of data and the follow-up. The first three are about a week's work.

sections.label: The article, condensed by another model
sections.line: ChatGPT's infographic condensed the article as the article proposes
sections.para: Dinis fed the article to ChatGPT for an infographic, which captured the five rows, the Cc change, the human-in-the-loop workflow, the four variants and the evaluation signals, inventing nothing. It is a reader's view rather than the sender's, and it was cheap: a condensation an agent makes in a minute and a person checks faster.

sections.label: Threads woven here
sections.line: Related articles on typed blocks, drafts and agent memory
sections.para: Links to Custom UIs are not the exception, with "send the summary, not the thread", and Replicating the agentic inbox, with the drafts role and no agent sending. Also linked: Memory is not a spectator sport, Six agents one inbox and its policy rows, and Agent Contact, whose messages carry the same decision, answer and status blocks.

sections.label: Sources
sections.line: Sources: the studies and pages cited
sections.para: RFC 1855, the Jargon File, the Email Charter, AR 25-50, Minto's Pyramid Principle, Nygard's decision records, Gmail, Copilot, Apple, Superhuman and Shortwave summary announcements, Microsoft's Work Trend Index, email summarisation research from 2004, 2007 and 2021, and MailFathom issue 1179. Figures use fictional threads; two research gaps are stated.
